home-and-zero.title: Home the machine & zero the Z axis

steps.text: Welcome to Training Mode. The machine will not move — every control is live, but a simulated tool answers instead of the real one. We'll practice the startup routine every job begins with: homing, then zeroing the Z axis.

First, the machine needs to find its fixed home position. In the Console's Machine card, press the highlighted Home XY button — a model of the simulated machine will pop up so you can watch what happens.
Watch the tool drive toward each proximity switch, back off, and creep back in slowly for an exact reading — first Y, then X. The Inputs lights in the top bar show each switch tripping.

The DRO now reads X 0.00  Y 0.00 — the machine knows where it is. Next: zeroing the Z axis, with two tools you'll find hanging on the real machine: the Z-zero plate — a flat aluminum plate with a wire on one end — and its grounding clip. Press the highlighted Home Z button to see how they're used.

This setup is YOUR job on a real machine: lay the plate flat under the bit, then snap the copper clip onto the bit — when the bit touches the plate it completes a circuit, and that's input 1. Watch it play out, then the bit finds the plate twice: a fast touch, and a slow one for accuracy. Z is set from the plate's known thickness.

That's the whole startup routine. Home XY once per session; zero the Z whenever the bit or material changes — and always unclip and stow the plate before you cut. This is exactly what you'll do on the real machine — the only difference is that it moves.

drive-the-machine.title: Drive the machine with the keypad

steps.text: Time to take the wheel. Driving the machine by hand is how you position the bit before every cut. That's your simulated tool on stage, and beside it a practice keypad — the same direction arrows you'll find on the real motion keypad.
The arrows jog the machine. Press and hold one of the XY arrows and watch the tool glide over the table. The position readout in the top bar follows along — let go and it stops instantly.
Now the fun part. Hold Z down until the Z readout goes below zero — below zero is inside the material, and the simulated bit will start carving the sheet.

You're cutting — now follow the path! I've painted a loop of blue squares on the sheet, starting where your bit is. Drive along it and clear every square — they carve away as you hit them. Either direction works. This is exactly what a job does: X and Y draw the toolpath.

Path cleared — nice driving! One last habit: on a real machine you'd never drag the bit sideways out of a cut without thinking — you always retract before traveling. Hold Z up until the readout is back above zero.

That's hand-driving: jog to position, plunge only on purpose, retract before you travel. On the real dashboard these same arrows live behind the highlighted keypad button in the top bar — it will feel like an old friend.

Time to cut something. Real work arrives as a cut file — your design software saves one, and the machine runs it. The routine is always the same three beats: load the file, preview it, cut it. This is the Job Manager, where all three happen.

Normally you'd drag your file anywhere onto this window to load it. I've gone ahead and loaded a practice file for you — Training practice cut just appeared in your queue, highlighted below. Loaded files simply wait in the queue; nothing moves until you run one.
Rule one: never cut a file you haven't looked at. The preview shows exactly where the tool will go before anything moves. Click the highlighted eye button on the job at the top of the queue.

This is the toolpath — every move the machine will make, drawn to scale on the table. Drag to spin it, scroll to zoom. Check two things on every job: it sits where you expect on the table, and the depths look right.
Looks good — let's go cut it. Press the highlighted X to close the preview and head back to the Job Manager.

The big play button runs the job at the top of the queue. On a real machine this is the moment of truth — bit tight, material clamped, dust collector on, Z zeroed. Here the simulator will take it. Press play.

Rolling! Watch the tool trace the same path you previewed — around the rectangle twice, deeper the second pass. The footer at the bottom tracks progress through the file, and the position readout follows along. On a real cut, this is where you stand: watching, within reach of pause.

Cut complete — and that's the whole cycle: load, preview, cut. It's the same three beats whether the file is this practice rectangle or a cabinet's worth of parts. I'll clear the practice file out of your queue on the way out.
